channel.title: Nature Human Behaviour
channel.description: Drawing from a broad spectrum of social and natural science disciplines, Nature Human Behaviour will publish research of outstanding significance into any aspect of human behaviour, its psychological, biological, and social bases. How do humans perceive, think, feel, decide, and act? How do they interact with their environments and others? How do these abilities develop and decline over the lifespan? How do they evolve and compare with other species? How do they vary among individuals, groups, and cultures? How are they shaped by socioeconomic and political factors? How are they affected by disease or deprivation? What interventions can influence individual behaviours or outcomes? The journal welcomes research from any discipline that provides significant original insight into these questions.

item.title: Effects of land acknowledgements on non-Indigenous audiences in Australia and the USA
item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 25 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02520-6

McNamee and Peyton find that land acknowledgements raise awareness of, but not curiosity about, Indigenous nations. These practices improve organizational reputations, but their effects on political attitudes and support for reparations are insignificant.
item.dc:title: Effects of land acknowledgements on non-Indigenous audiences in Australia and the USA
item.dc:creator: Lachlan McNamee
Kyle Peyton

item.title: Why girls have worse mental health than boys
item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 22 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02577-3

Analyses of data from more than 3,000 adolescents found that loneliness and desire for thinness contribute to the higher prevalence of depressive symptoms and suicidal ideation among girls than in boys. Young people’s perspectives informed the pathways that were investigated.
item.dc:title: Why girls have worse mental health than boys
item.dc:source: Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 2026-09-22; | doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02577-3

item.title: What chimpanzees at war have taught me about being human
item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 21 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02601-6

Seeing a deadly ‘civil war’ unfold among chimpanzees has been a painful experience for John Mitani. His decades of watching wild great apes now evoke his family’s experience with xenophobia. But to him, the war highlights what makes humans unique: not our conflicts, but our unparalleled capacity for tolerance and cooperation.
item.dc:title: What chimpanzees at war have taught me about being human

item.title: Meritocracy and inequality acceptance
item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 21 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02567-5

The idea of meritocracy — that income differences should reflect performance rather than luck or inherited privilege — can be used to justify inequality. Yet people who consider meritocracy to be fair may disagree about redistribution. Understanding these disagreements can help to reduce polarization.
item.dc:title: Meritocracy and inequality acceptance
item.dc:creator: Alexander W. Cappelen
Bertil Tungodden

item.title: There is no clear target for replication rates
item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 21 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02602-5

Is a 50% replication rate too high, too low or just right? We need a target replication rate to answer this question. Here, I evaluate two potential target rates, the ‘optimal’ replication rate and the ‘expected’ replication rate, and I call for an educational intervention to better appreciate their limitations.
item.dc:title: There is no clear target for replication rates
item.dc:creator: Mark Rubin
item.dc:source: Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 2026-09-21; | doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02602-5

item.title: Understanding the structural and psychological bases of inequality
item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 21 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02600-7

Inequalities in education, health, technology and social status are often studied in isolation. This Focus issue shows how these inequalities are interconnected in the real world, and how competing views of fairness shape the responses to them. To reduce inequality, we need more research on the drivers: how complex interactions among individual beliefs, institutions, technologies and environments widen the gaps or create opportunities for change.
item.dc:title: Understanding the structural and psychological bases of inequality
item.dc:source: Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 2026-09-21; | doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02600-7
